name: Executive order of November 15, 1883 enlarging the Gila River Reservation for the Pima and Maricopa
citation: Executive order of November 15, 1883 (1 Kappler 808; Royce area 651)
nations: Akimel O'odham (Pima) and Piipaash (Maricopa), today the Gila River Indian Community and the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community
promises: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It set apart a large addition to the Pima and Maricopa reserve, running from the Salt River at the corner of the June 14, 1879 addition east and south to the reserve of August 31, 1876, then west to the Gila and Salt River meridian (Royce p. 914, area 651).
The Indian Claims Commission found this was the greatest single addition, enlarging the reservation to almost its present 372,000 acres (Docket 228, additional finding 26).

breaches.what: The Commission held that this order manifested the Government's intention to assert dominion over the whole Pima-Maricopa aboriginal tract, and fixed November 15, 1883 as the date the United States took their title to all of it not already entered by settlers; lands entered earlier were taken on their dates of entry.

breaches.what: In its opinion the Commission found the earlier additions were meant to grant the Pima and Maricopa the land they occupied, but that with the 1883 enlargement came an apparent attempt at a final settlement of Pima land claims and an unequivocal exercise of dominion over the public domain after it.

landTaken: The Commission found the Pima-Maricopa aboriginal area was approximately 3 3/4 million acres (additional finding 26); the acreage taken on November 15, 1883, net of lands entered earlier, was not stated in the decisions opened.
compensation: Congress refers to judgment funds awarded to the Gila River Indian Community in Docket No. 228 and to a distribution plan published at 52 Fed. Reg. 6887 (March 5, 1987) (Public Law 108-22, section 201). The amount was not found in a source opened.
today: Congress set conditions on the Docket 228 judgment fund plan in 2003 (Public Law 108-22). The Gila River Indian Community and the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community hold the reservations.

nationVoice.summary: The Community says Congress set apart the first reservation in Arizona for it in 1859, and that in the 1870s and 1880s upstream diversions and dams built by non-Native farmers cut off its Gila River water and largely wiped out its farming, followed by decades of famine.

openQuestions: The land the Commission found taken lies OUTSIDE this order's addition (Royce area 651, which the order reserved). The order is the act the Commission dated the taking by, so the finding is about this order, but the map polygon shows the land kept, not the land lost. This is the same pattern as the Hualapai (1883) and Hopi (1882) orders.
This is the only queue record that carries the Docket 228 taking; cession-1879-06-14-maricopa-pima mentions it only under today.

The final judgment amount in Docket 228 (the case moved to the Court of Claims in 1978) was not found in a source opened. The 1972 order denying rehearing (OSU id 1143) is listed but was not read in full.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. A presidential order in 1883 enlarged the Gila River Reservation for the Pima and Maricopa to almost its present 372,000 acres.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found that with this order the United States took Pima-Maricopa title to the rest of their aboriginal land, not yet settled, without paying for it.
plain.today: Judgment funds were awarded in Docket 228 and Congress set conditions on their distribution in 2003. The amount was not found.
